name: Kosmos 419
short_status: Reached Earth parking orbit on 10 May 1971, but its Blok D upper stage never restarted because the wrong ignition time had been loaded into the onboard computer. It reentered on 12 May 1971.
tagline: USSR · Soviet Union · Orbiter · 1971 · Reaching Mars Failure
stats: the ignition delay loaded into the computer, instead of a few tens of minutes
Soviet Mars spacecraft launched in the 1971 window

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 10 May 1971 at 16:58:42 UTC (19:58:42 Moscow), Proton-K (8K82K no. 253-01) with a Blok D upper stage (11S824 no. 1101L), from Site 81 Pad 23 at Baikonur. The Russian-language accounts give the time as 20:24 Moscow, about 25 minutes later; the 16:58:42 UTC figure is used here because Siddiqi, McDowell's GCAT and the launch catalogues agree on it

facts.label: Designations
facts.value: 3MS No. 170, also written M-71S. NSSDCA lists it as M-71S No. 170 and some catalogues call it Mars 1971C. The public name Kosmos 419 was a cover: Soviet practice was to give a Kosmos number to any planetary probe that ended up stuck in Earth orbit

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 4,549 kg according to Siddiqi and McDowell's catalogue, with a dry mass of 2,164 kg and about 17,909 kg for the whole stack including the Blok D. NSSDCA and Russian Wikipedia both give 4,650 kg, which is the figure Siddiqi assigns to Mars 2

facts.label: Built by
facts.value: NPO Lavochkin (GSMZ imeni Lavochkina), with the KTDU-425 main engine

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: Orbiter only, with no descent module. A cylindrical propulsion tank block, a toroidal instrument compartment, deployable solar panels, thermal control radiators and antennas. It could also have relayed data from the landers carried by Mars 2 and Mars 3

facts.label: Why it existed
facts.value: The 1971 plan originally called for two orbiter and lander pairs. A third, lighter, orbiter-only spacecraft was added specifically to reach Mars orbit ahead of the American Mariner H and Mariner I, and to measure the planet's position precisely so the two landers could be aimed correctly

facts.label: Onboard computer
facts.value: The M-71 series carried the first onboard digital computer flown on a Soviet interplanetary spacecraft. Siddiqi names it the S-530 and describes it as a simplified Argon-11, the machine flown on the 7K-L1 Zond craft; the Russian account describes the relationship the other way round, calling the L-1 unit the simplified one. Its job included computing the lander entry settings

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: Fluxgate magnetometer, infrared radiometer, infrared photometer, RIEP-2801 multi-channel plasma spectrometer, visible photometer, radiometer, ultraviolet photometer, cosmic ray detector, D-127 charged particle traps, an imaging system using the Vega and Zufar cameras, and the French Stereo-1 radio astronomy experiment

facts.label: Parking orbit
facts.value: 145 by 159 km at 51.5 degrees inclination with an 87.4 minute period according to Siddiqi and the Russian technical account. Published figures vary widely: NSSDCA says 174 by 159 km at 51.4 degrees, McDowell's catalogue says 126 by 191 km at 51.46 degrees (the Russian Wikipedia infobox has 126 by 191 km at 51.4 degrees), English Wikipedia says 134 by 187 km

facts.label: The failure
facts.value: The Blok D never restarted for the trans-Mars burn. A wrong value for the ignition time had been entered into the onboard computer, and because of an error in one digit the engine was set to start after roughly 150 hours instead of the few tens of minutes the flight program called for

facts.label: A competing account
facts.value: Perminov, Lavochkin's lead designer for the Mars and Venus spacecraft, writes that the tracking ship in the Gulf of Guinea saw no ignition, that telemetry over the Yevpatoria station in Crimea showed no start command had been issued at all, and that an operator had entered an eight-digit code command in reverse order. He also dates the launch 5 May 1971, which is wrong, so his chronology should be treated with care

facts.label: Reentry
facts.value: 12 May 1971, two days after launch. McDowell's catalogue gives the decay as roughly 20:10 UTC on 12 May

facts.label: Catalogue identifiers
facts.value: COSPAR designation 1971-042A, US satellite catalogue number 5221

facts.label: The Stereo-1 problem
facts.value: France had been promised that two copies of its Stereo-1 decametric radio experiment would fly to Mars in 1971. One was on Kosmos 419 and burned up, but the mission officially did not exist, so when the second Mars spacecraft appeared to have a non-working Stereo the Soviet side let the French believe it was an instrument fault

facts.label: The fix
facts.value: The cause was found quickly and the computer program was corrected. Mars 2 launched nine days later on 19 May 1971 and Mars 3 on 28 May 1971, and both reached Mars

facts.label: What was lost
facts.value: Without an early orbiter, the Soviet programme lost both the radio beacon and the improved measurement of Mars's position that Mars 2 and Mars 3 were to have used when aiming their landers, and had to fall back on an optical angle-measuring system designed as a backup in 1970

timeline: Mariner 8 is destroyed by its Centaur upper stage, removing one of the two American orbiters that Kosmos 419 had been added to the plan to beat
16:58:42 UTC: launch from Site 81 Pad 23. The Proton performs and the spacecraft reaches a 145 by 159 km parking orbit at 51.5 degrees
Roughly an hour later, over the Gulf of Guinea, the Soviet tracking ship sees no sign that the Blok D has ignited
Minutes afterwards the stack passes over the Yevpatoria control station in Crimea and telemetry shows that no engine start command was ever issued
The spacecraft and its dead upper stage reenter and burn up, two days after launch
Mars 2 launches with the corrected onboard computer program
Mars 3 launches, carrying the second Stereo-1 experiment
Mariner 9 launches, the surviving half of the American pair
Mariner 9 enters Mars orbit and becomes the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, the outcome Kosmos 419 was built to prevent
Mars 2 arrives. Its orbiter enters Mars orbit; its lander is sent in at too steep an angle by faulty settings from the onboard computer and is destroyed on impact
Mars 3 arrives and lands, transmitting for a matter of seconds from the surface

images.caption: A large labelled drawing of the M-71C spacecraft with Russian callouts and a thirteen item English key, naming the astro navigation optics, the instrument module, the magnetometer, the stereo antenna, the high gain parabolic antenna, the low gain cone antennas, the propulsion tanks, the thermal radiators, the attitude and stabilisation nozzles and the solar panels. Perminov captions this figure as the M-71C, the vehicle the Soviets flew as Kosmos 419; NSSDCA hosts the same scan under a Mars 2 and Mars 3 filename because the orbiters were built on the same bus.
images.credit: NASA/NSSDCA, from V. G. Perminov, The Difficult Road to Mars, NASA Monographs in Aerospace History No. 15, 1999
